rewrites.summary:
Pakistan is dangerous for trans travellers — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act is described as one of the most progressive pieces of legislation internationally, but the national religious court (the Shariat Court) gutted it in 2023, declaring provisions "un-Islamic". Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi, the largest city of the country, 267 violence cases were documented in one state/province (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions). No trans-traveller-specific border friction or death in custody is documented. The 2020 rules introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but how document markers are treated at border crossings is undocumented.

For partner travel, no relationship or partner recognition is documented, so partner-based protections should not be assumed. The severity of social and police violence is the dominant risk.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The 2023 religious-court ruling is under appeal to the top court of the country, so the legal status quo may shift while a visit is being planned — litigation flux, not a current enforcement risk.

Neighbour comparisons: unlike a neighbouring country (Malaysia), there is no cross-dressing criminalisation here; unlike two neighbouring countries (the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia) where deaths in custody and border mistreatment of trans travellers were documented, no analogous trans-traveller case is documented here.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2018 Act's third-gender recognition (gutted by the religious court in 2023, under appeal) and the hijra community's legal recognition are resident-facing; the 267 documented violence cases and jirga case-closures describe residents' situation.

Third-gender recognition has existed since 2009, a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety operates in Lahore, and civil society is active — all resident-facing facts a visitor would not directly rely on.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain regions affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the precise criminal status of consensual same-sex conduct — the statutes cited in the sources differ and definitions are unclear — remains ambiguous; no prosecutions were documented.

Unresolved: how identity documents are treated at border crossings ('X' recognition-marker practice is undocumented).

blindSourceSummaries: A newswire report (Nov 2024): gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near the largest city — the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

A public broadcaster (Sep 2025): police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway in the largest city — the latest in a continuing pattern of lethal violence; estimates put the number of transgender citizens facing social exclusion and abuse at hundreds of thousands.

A local legal-aid organisation's policy brief: despite notable legal advances (the 2018 Act), protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice — the central challenge is implementation failure, not absence of law; the brief makes custody and police-safeguard recommendations.

A foreign home ministry's official country guidance on sexual orientation and gender identity (Nov 2025): trans people are protected under the 2018 Act though the national religious court declared provisions 'un-Islamic' in 2023; consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under an older statute (two years to life, definition unclear, male-to-male acts), with only men affected per a rights organisation; people are unlikely to face persecution by the authorities.

An international human-rights organisation (May 2023): the national religious court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the 2018 Act is 'a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group'; the organisation had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards.

A national daily (Oct 2025): analysis of the gap between law and reality — the 2018 Act affirmed self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 rules introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but trans people still face violence, street harassment, landlord rejection, hospital dismissal, and suspicion or ridicule at police stations.

A decriminalisation news outlet (Feb 2026): a wave of violence has left trans people afraid to go out — a night-time shooting at two activists (three bullets fired through a door, narrow escape); a senior legislator proposes a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control official gender identity — an active retrograde legislative push.

An opinion analysis (May 2023) of the national religious court's verdict on the 2018 Act: the court ruled that sections on identity, self-perceived gender identity, and inheritance do not conform with the petitioners' reading of religious principles, and speculated the Act could facilitate rape or sexual assault of women by men 'disguised' as transgender women — framing echoing anti-trans moral panics from abroad.

A foreign-affairs magazine (Jul 2025): the 2018 Act was hailed as a legislative turning point — granting the right to self-identify and protection from discrimination in education, employment, and healthcare — yet citizens are 'legally recognised, socially forsaken': statutory rights not matching lived status.

A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report: same-sex conduct criminalised under an older statute; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.
rewrites.notes: Restructure of the existing summary into the four rule-6 fields; neighbour comparisons (Malaysia, UAE, Indonesia) and the Supreme-Court appeal moved to tangentialFactors; localsOnly preserved and expanded with the current resident-facing items; no new facts beyond the supplied claims.

rewrites.summary:
The Philippines is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), the SOGIE Equality Bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: A national anti-discrimination equality bill has been stalled in the national legislature for 25 years, and no national legal gender recognition law exists; the 2025 killings are being cited by activists as an urgent reminder for the bill's passage. This is national legislation flux that may colour a visit, not a direct travel restriction.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The absent national legal gender recognition law, the 25-year-stalled equality bill, and the commission's lack of enforcement power are resident-facing; the 2025 killings and the earlier documented student discrimination in schools affect residents primarily.

Deep cultural traditions of gender diversity (bakla, tomboy) and the capital's Pride and nightlife scene are resident-facing cultural facts a visitor can observe but not rely on legally.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical treatment of identity documents at borders is not documented, and the sources do not detail how bathroom and fitting-room policies at venues are enforced.

blindSourceSummaries: An international legal-rights organisation's country overview: a 2023 update to a professional code bars sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination of clients; openly gay and bisexual people allowed in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017; a 2001 clerical-error law blocks administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people (a judicial order required), and a 2008 top-court ruling bars legal-gender change even after surgery.

A news outlet (Jun 2025): two killings in days — an 18-year-old trans woman found dead in a river after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic the same day; an LGBT alliance says the cases are an urgent reminder to pass the equality bill, stuck in the national legislature for 25 years.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (403); the underlying national newspaper report (May 2025) covers a foreigner arrested for raping a trans woman in a provincial area.

An entertainment-news site (Apr 2024): a drag artist was physically struck on stage by a man from the crowd at an outdoor concert — the artist called the attack traumatic and urged passage of the equality bill; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTIQ community.

A local magazine explainer: 25 years of legislative inaction on the equality bill; patchwork protections that do exist — anti-discrimination ordinances in provinces and cities and several national laws punishing transphobic and homophobic slurs with fines and sensitivity training.

An independent news site: trans people demand legal gender recognition — a bill would let applicants, including minors with consent, choose markers beyond male and female; the national human-rights commission called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'; allies plan to endorse the bill to the next congress session.

A travel-safety platform's page on the capital (2026): the capital rated 'Generally Safe' for LGB travellers but only 'Exercise Caution' for trans travellers; same-sex relations never criminalised, deep gender-diversity traditions and a vibrant Pride scene, but the equality bill (filed in 2000) is stuck and there is no marriage equality; accessibility caveat: most of the rail system lacks step-free entrances.

An international human-rights organisation's report (Jun 2017) on discrimination against LGBT students in this country: bullying and discrimination across schools, with the law short on remedies at the time — basis-level evidence of the school climate for gender-diverse youth.

rewrites.summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: No trans-specific killing has been documented here, in contrast to several neighbouring countries. The September 2025 cancellations of the flagship Pride march and other LGBTQ events in the largest city — a national-level policy signal that may colour a visit — are adjacent climate rather than a direct travel restriction.
rewrites.localsOnly: The stalled Gender Affirmation Law, the documented conversion efforts, and the healthcare discrimination barriers are resident-facing — these govern residents' access to recognition, safety, and care rather than a visitor's experience.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Political controls of one ruling party, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon or monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical effect of the stalled recognition law on border document checks is not documented in the sources.

blindSourceSummaries: A foreign public broadcaster (late Sep/Oct 2025): the largest city abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — a human-rights specialist calls it worrying signs of a clampdown on LGBTIQ rights; the piece notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions without legal recognition.

An international LGBTIQ organisation's country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 is still not implemented — obstacles persist to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026; same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; a ministry declared (Aug 2022) that same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders.

An international human-rights organisation's 2025 country report: rights of LGBTI people lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; alongside wider repression — vague penal-code articles used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025.

A research-institute study (Oct 2024): exploration of the lived experiences of conversion efforts among LGBTIQ people in this country — documents their experiences and forms, with a comprehensive data-needs analysis.

A UN country-team feature (Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially women from outlying state/province and minority groups — framed as a case for accessible legal recognition.

A local news site (Jun 2023): a Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist; same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised.

A foreign refugee-board information request (Jun 2022): no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds; multi-source briefing on treatment by society and authorities in the two largest cities across education, employment, housing, and health care.

Government media (Nov 2018): the national assembly was expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; a recognition draft law was still under consideration years later.

rewrites.summary:
Peru is a country that demands real caution for trans visitors, with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence, but no criminalisation of trans identity. The national legislature approved (February–April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated restriction comparable to bans passed in other countries. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed — trans women most affected. In one documented case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025), an unprecedented conviction. An official decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024) before being walked back after mass protests.

For a visitor: no border friction or criminalisation, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure whenever public facilities are used. Same-sex or partner recognition does not exist, so marriage-based protections cannot be assumed.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The bathroom ban is a nationally-legislated restriction that sources compare to similar limitations passed in parts of other countries (for example, bathroom restrictions in some states of the USA and the guidance of a British equalities body).

National-level legal and policy developments colour the climate around a visit: an anti-equality decree struck down in July 2025 by a court in the capital, congressional bills restricting bathroom use and inclusive signage, and a 2017 removal of hate-crime protections from the penal code.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The court-based legal gender recognition process (expensive, years-long, no self-identification law) is resident-facing; the 54 killings and the torture case concern residents.

The consumer-protection dismissal, the official decree classifying trans identity as a "mental disorder", and its walk-back after mass protests are resident-facing facts a visitor would not encounter directly.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: how the bathroom ban is enforced in practice at public facilities and how it applies to visitors is not documented in the sources.

blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (Feb 2025): a national-legislature committee in this country approved unanimously a bill threatening trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and quotas in public office.

A university human-rights institute analysis: the bathroom-restriction provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites a regional human-rights court advisory opinion that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee full rights.

A regional news platform (Jul 2024): hate crimes rose and trans women are the most affected; recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; a 2012 university study found the majority of trans women in the two largest cities work in sex work.

A foreign broadcaster's world service (Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman — this country's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the first torture-by-discrimination case of a regional human-rights court in the region's history.
A news outlet (Dec 2025): the officers sentenced to 17 years for the rape and torture of a trans woman — the sentence landing nearly 20 years after the attack.

An international human-rights organisation (May 2025): an April-2025 law mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles enable censorship; the organisation says child protection is used as a pretext for repression and scapegoating.

An international human-rights organisation (Jun 2024): the health system walked back anti-trans guidance — authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity'.

An international LGBTIQ organisation's country overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a court in the capital ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; an April-2025 law restricts restrooms by 'biological sex'; an April-2025 law lets authorities revoke registrations on public-order grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually.

A foreign solidarity-group briefing (Apr 2025): a week of setbacks — the national legislature approved bills banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; a media personality publicly harassed the first openly lesbian member of the national legislature; pressure continues against abortion rights.

An activist news digest (May 2017): the national legislature voted to strip LGBT protections from the new penal code's hate-crime provisions — carried after a constitutional-committee vote and amid a claimed petition with a million signatures; the outcome left the country among only a few in its region lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

rewrites.summary:
Qatar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf — its region. An international human-rights organisation interviewed four transgender women arrested by the security department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in the capital, Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Same-sex conduct is also criminalised, so a partner travelling with you carries the same exposure. Arrests continued even as this country hosted the 2022 World Cup — a major international sporting event — under international scrutiny.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: During 2022, arrests continued even as the country hosted the 2022 World Cup — a major international sporting event — under global scrutiny, showing that enforcement is not moderated by international attention. The current sources compare the enforcement record of this country with neighbouring countries and place it as the most severe in the region.
rewrites.localsOnly: The current sources record no resident-specific facts beyond the risk assessment already given — the documented arrests of people based solely on their gender expression in public places describe a pattern that applies alike to residents and to visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Migrant-worker abuses and the sponsorship labour system, and general human-rights concerns, affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: how trans visitors are treated at border entry and document checks is not documented in the sources; the documented detentions begin after entry, in public places.

The reported physical detransition rests on a single documented account and could not be independently verified from the current sources.

An LGBTIQ news outlet (2018): taboo around homosexuality in this country — an essay by a gay citizen drew extreme reactions; commentators on expected conduct during the upcoming global sporting event; no legal change.

rewrites.summary:
Bahrain is a place to avoid entirely for trans visitors, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the region. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in this country since 1976 and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression; a foreign government's official guidance notes that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in the capital on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker, showing that corrected identity documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

rewrites.summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these countries."

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Comparisons with neighbours: sources note the explicit anti-trans statute is unusual in its region, and the traveller's public warning told others "do not go to these countries." The national enforcement pattern is active — the 2018 arrests were publicly announced after private-party photos circulated on social media, showing active monitoring of gender non-conformity.
rewrites.localsOnly: The current sources record no resident-specific facts beyond the enforcement pattern already described in the summary — the 2018 arrests and the anti-trans statute apply to residents and visitors alike; no local cultural or resident-life facts are documented.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

An online news outlet (Feb 2023): a non-binary visitor at the capital's airport says friends cleared immigration but she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers — first-hand evidence of border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

An international human-rights organisation's regional report (Apr 2018): the 2018 penal code added a provision punishing any man who appears to dress in women's clothing, alongside the existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGB organising; includes a regional comparison of imitation laws.

A law-journal article (2012) distinguishing homosexual acts from homosexual persons: in some countries guided by religious law, acts are criminalised (even capitally) while identity alone is not — scholarly context for the legal-religious framework of this country.

rewrites.summary:
Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveller-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues under the free-movement rules of the regional union this country belongs to, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022 a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside an LGBT bar in the capital — classified as the country's first modern terrorist attack. The national authorities responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital.

For a visitor: no legal exposure and functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against transgender recognition. The sources document no marriage or partner-recognition protections, so partner-based expectations should not be assumed.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified after the 2022 attack rather than receding: the elected local legislature advanced a bill that would make legal gender recognition impossible (on a genetic-test-only basis) — national-level legislative flux that colours a visit without being a current restriction.
rewrites.localsOnly: The 40-year-old medicalised legal gender recognition regime and the LGR-ban bill are resident-facing; the proposed constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable are likewise resident-facing climate signals.

Roma discrimination (an ethnic minority) is out of scope for this record; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
